client: I've been really stressed out lately about this family reunion that's coming up next month. Just thinking about it makes my heart race — like, I can feel my chest tighten and my thoughts start spiraling. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to make it any easier to actually show up there.
therapist: It sounds like even just thinking about the reunion brings up a lot of tension in your body, which tells me this feels pretty significant for you. That worry about whether talking will actually help is really understandable — and it's actually a great thing to name right at the start. I'm curious, when your thoughts start spiraling about the reunion, what's the kind of thought that tends to show up first?

client: The first thought that usually hits me is something like, "Everyone's going to notice how much I've pulled away from the family over the past few years." And then it just snowballs from there — I start imagining all these awkward silences or people asking why I never call, and I don't have a good answer for any of it. It's like I already feel guilty before I've even walked through the door.
therapist: That pre-emptive guilt is such a heavy thing to carry — you're essentially putting yourself on trial before anyone has even said a word to you. It's worth gently noticing that your mind is treating these imagined reactions as facts, when really they're predictions your anxious brain is generating to try to "prepare" you. What evidence do you actually have that people will respond that way, versus what might you be filling in yourself?

client: I mean, I hear what you're saying, and logically I get it — but it's hard to separate that out when my aunt literally texted me last Christmas asking why I'd gone so quiet. That feels like pretty real evidence to me, not just something I'm making up. So it's not totally in my head, right?
therapist: You're absolutely right that your aunt's text is real — I don't want to dismiss that, and it makes sense that it stuck with you. But it's worth exploring what that moment actually tells us: she reached out, which could mean she noticed the distance *and* still wanted connection, rather than judgment. What do you think she was really looking for when she sent that message?

client: Okay, maybe she was reaching out because she missed me, I can kind of see that. But even if that's true, it almost makes it worse — like, now I feel guilty for not responding better to her, on top of everything else. It's hard to reframe it as something warm when my gut reaction is just more shame.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you could open up to that possibility, even a little — and it makes sense that it immediately brought up another layer of guilt, because that's often how shame works, it finds a new foothold. What I'm noticing is that you're holding yourself to a standard where even someone missing you becomes evidence against you, which is worth slowing down on. Where do you think that tendency to turn warmth into self-blame comes from for you?

client: Honestly, I think it goes back pretty far — like, I grew up in a family where you were kind of expected to show up and be present, and when you weren't, it was noticed and commented on. So I guess I internalized this idea that pulling back means you're failing the people you love. But I'm not sure digging into where it comes from actually changes how it feels when I'm standing in that reunion hall next month.
therapist: That's a really important insight — you've carried this belief that distance equals failure for a long time, and it makes complete sense it feels so automatic now. You're also right that understanding where something comes from doesn't instantly dissolve it, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. But I'm wondering — if a close friend told you they'd pulled back from family for a few years, would you see them as failing the people they love, or might you understand it differently?

client: I'd probably be really understanding with a friend — like, I'd assume they had their reasons and I wouldn't think less of them for it. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just doesn't land the same way, it feels almost like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. I don't know if that's me being hard on myself or if there's actually a real difference between my situation and a hypothetical friend's.
therapist: That gap you're noticing — where compassion flows easily toward others but feels almost suspicious when you turn it on yourself — is actually one of the most common and telling patterns we see, and it's worth taking seriously. The feeling that self-compassion means "letting yourself off the hook" is itself a belief worth examining, because understanding your own reasons isn't the same as saying your choices had no impact. What do you think would actually happen inside you if you allowed yourself the same understanding you'd give a friend — would it feel like giving up, or might it free up some space to do something different?

client: I think if I'm being honest, it might free up some space — like, maybe I'd stop spending so much energy dreading the reunion and actually think about how I want to show up there. But there's also this fear that if I'm too easy on myself, I'll just keep avoiding and nothing will actually change. I guess I'm not sure self-compassion and actually doing the hard thing can coexist.
therapist: There's something really hopeful in what you just said — you can already sense that releasing some of this weight might actually move you *toward* the reunion rather than away from it, which suggests self-compassion and action aren't as opposed as they feel. In fact, harsh self-judgment often keeps us stuck in shame loops rather than motivating change, while self-compassion can create the safety needed to take a real risk. So I'm curious — when you imagine showing up to that reunion from a place of "I have reasons for the distance and I want to reconnect," rather than "I'm guilty and need to prove myself," how does that version of you behave differently?

client: That version of me probably walks in without immediately scanning the room for judgment, maybe even initiates a conversation with my aunt instead of waiting to be confronted. But honestly, just imagining it feels kind of fragile — like it's a nice idea in theory but I'm worried the second someone says something even slightly pointed, I'll collapse right back into that guilty, defensive place. I don't know how to make that more grounded version of me actually stick when things get real.
therapist: That image of you initiating with your aunt rather than bracing for confrontation is genuinely significant — and the fragility you're feeling around it is real, not a sign it won't work. What you're describing is actually something we can prepare for concretely: if someone says something pointed, having a grounded response ready in advance can be the difference between collapsing into old patterns and staying anchored in that more compassionate version of yourself. What's one thing someone might say at the reunion that feels most likely to knock you off balance, so we can think through how that grounded version of you might actually handle it?

client: Probably the thing that would hit hardest is someone saying something like, "We never hear from you anymore, it's like you don't care about this family." Just typing that out makes my stomach drop a little. I can see how having a response ready might help, but I'm also worried that if I rehearse something it'll come out sounding scripted and defensive, which might make things worse instead of better.
therapist: That sentence clearly carries a lot of weight for you, and it makes sense your body reacted just to typing it — it cuts right to the core of that fear of being seen as someone who stopped caring. The good news is that preparing a response doesn't have to mean memorizing a script; it can just mean getting clear on what's *true* for you, so that when the moment comes, you're drawing from something real rather than performing. What would you actually want someone like your aunt to understand about why you pulled back, if you could say it honestly and without shame?

client: I think what I'd want her to understand is that pulling back wasn't about not caring — it was more like I was going through a really hard period and I didn't know how to show up as anything other than a mess, so I just... disappeared instead. Saying that out loud actually feels different from the guilt spiral, like it's more honest and less about failing. But I'm scared that even if I say something true and vulnerable like that, it might not land the way I mean it, and I'll just end up feeling more exposed and misunderstood than before.
therapist: What you just articulated is really profound — "I didn't know how to show up as anything other than a mess, so I disappeared" is honest, human, and actually quite hard to misunderstand if someone is listening with any openness at all. The fear of being exposed and still misunderstood is real, and vulnerability does carry that risk — but notice that saying it out loud just now felt different from the guilt spiral, which suggests it's already doing something for *you* regardless of how anyone else receives it. How might it change things if you went into that conversation holding onto that — that speaking your truth has value even if the other person's response isn't perfect?
